children: “A known devil is better than an unknown one” is the common saying. For Onida, familiarity may no longer be enough. Its ‘devil’ may need to take an unfamiliar turn as a crusader taking on problems that appliance buyers have learnt to tolerate — from hard water damaging washing machines to air conditioners that force households to buy separate heaters during winter, and obscure warranties and repeat repairs.

That would give a contemporary cause to a mascot introduced in 1984 with the tagline “Neighbour’s Envy, Owner’s Pride”, but repeatedly retired, revived and reinvented since. Harish Bijoor, brand strategy specialist and founder of Harish Bijoor Consults Inc, argues that Onida’s devil needs precisely such a role for a new generation.

“Make the devil the Tukaram Mundhe of consumer durables activism,” Bijoor says, invoking the bureaucrat known for taking on entrenched systems. His argument: Don’t make the devil Onida’s salesman; make him the consumer’s advocate.
Sanjay Sarma, Principal Consultant and Founder of SSARMA Consults, agrees these are the “newer problems” that Onida could own and almost “fix the plumbing for your life”.
Origins in envy

Giraj Sharma, Co-founder of BehindTheMoon Consultants, who joined Onida in 1985 and spent 12 years heading marketing, recalls that colour TVs were scarce enough for families to gather at neighbours’ homes that had them. The envy existed before the advertising did; Onida’s tagline captured that tension, and the devil gave it a face.
Onida’s brand manual now moves him “From Envy to Intelligence”, replacing “I want what they have” with “Maybe there is a smarter choice”.
The stakes are bigger than just another advertising comeback. At its peak in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Onida commanded 18–20 per cent of India’s colour TV market.

Revenue fell about 45 per cent from ₹1,192.17 crore in FY22 to roughly ₹660 crore in FY26. Under Onida 5.0, its devil is recast as an “intelligent provocateur”, darker, sharper and more premium — one who “never follows”, “never attacks” and “never boasts without reason”. His confidence, the manual says, comes from “product truth”.
Renaming and Rebooting
But while Onida has defined how its resurrected devil should behave, it’s less clear which consumer problem he is out to solve.

For “Onida rewired” the company has raised ₹149.52 crore, exited contract manufacturing and renamed MIRC Electronics as Onida Electronics. It is widening its retail reach, pushing 100-inch QD mini-LED TVs and smart inverter ACs, and targeting over 5 per cent of the premium TV and AC markets within three years.

Its management has spoken of increasing revenue five-fold over five years, implying about ₹3,300 crore at a 38 per cent CAGR. Early signs show Q1 FY27 revenue up 30 per cent year-on-year to ₹182–185 crore, but one quarter does not establish a turnaround.
The Bosch playbook

The man attempting this feat has partly done it before. Gunjan Srivastava, who took charge of Onida after heading BSH Home Appliances in India, had earlier adapted Bosch and Siemens products to local conditions, such as launching 7 kg washing machines when 6 kg models dominated.
Onida presents a reverse challenge. Srivastava isn’t bringing a global power brand to India; he is trying to make an established domestic brand matter again amidst fierce competition.

Product comparisons illustrate the gap. Onida TVs offer Google and Fire TV platforms, but rivals differentiate around gaming and audio. IFB, Whirlpool and Samsung market washing machines with hard water solutions, while Onida lacks a prominent equivalent. Its ACs offer inverter cooling but haven’t made all-weather operation a core proposition.

Warranty is another test. Onida’s IRIS inverter AC offers one year on product and five on the compressor; its washing machines offer two years on product and five on the motor. Rivals advertise longer protection. For a returning brand, service reassurance carries unusual weight.
Sarma calls it Onida’s “Bata problem”: Recognition survives, but recognition isn’t preference. Onida “doesn’t need to introduce itself; it needs to reintroduce why it matters”.
The changed neighbour
Buyers now instantly compare specifications, reviews and prices across digital marketplaces. Envy today means bigger screens, smoother gaming or better value.

Sharma’s take is starker: “If you don’t give good quality, you’re not even playing. If you don’t give good service, you’re not even in the game.” The generation Onida needs to win over may neither remember the devil nor view television as a traditional broadcast box. Screens now serve OTT, consoles and smart setups, competing with laptops and projectors.

Bijoor argues that Onida’s devil cannot return merely as nostalgia. A younger consumer needs a reason to care today. That brings him back to the Tukaram Mundhe proposition: Give the devil a contemporary 2026 problem worth fighting.
The devil’s final test
Distribution can put Onida back on the shelf, but Onida 5.0 must make consumers want the brand again.

businessline sought an interview with Srivastava on strategy and product differentiation; the company provided product images and a brand manual instead. That manual claims the Onida devil’s confidence comes from “product truth”. After four years of revenue decline, Onida must prove its mascot is still rooted in a real consumer tension.
Sharma reduces the test to one line: “If the envy is gone, the entire premise of having a devil is gone.”

title: Onida rewired: The devil is in the details
